references.text: The preceding verse asks the question "What is the kingdom of God like?" which the parable of the mustard seed in verse 19 answers ([ref:Luk 13:18|Luke 13:18]).
The parallel passage in Matthew's Gospel where Jesus tells the same parable of the mustard seed growing into a tree where the birds of heaven build nests ([ref:Matt 13:31-32|Matthew 13:31-32]).
The parallel passage in Mark's Gospel with the parable of the mustard seed, which grows up and becomes larger than all garden plants ([ref:Mark 4:30-32|Mark 4:30-32]).

Ezekiel's prophecy that the Lord will plant a branch on a high mountain in Israel, and it shall become a glorious cedar tree where birds of every kind dwell in the shade of its branches – an image of the kingdom of God growing from something small to something great ([ref:Esek 17:23-24|Ezekiel 17:23-24]).

The image of the great tree where the birds of heaven build nests in its branches, used concerning Assyria as a mighty cedar – the same imagery that Jesus uses for the kingdom of God ([ref:Esek 31:6|Ezekiel 31:6]).

Nebuchadnezzar's dream of the great tree that grew and became powerful, with the birds of heaven dwelling in its branches – a related image of a kingdom growing to greatness ([ref:Dan 4:10-12|Daniel 4:10-12]).
The birds of heaven that dwell by the water sources and sing among the branches – a similar natural image as in Jesus' parable ([ref:Sal 104:12|Psalms 104:12]).

Jesus speaks about faith as a mustard seed – the smallest beginning can lead to great results, which reflects the point of the parable about growth from the very least ([ref:Matt 17:20|Matthew 17:20]).
The following parable about yeast further explains the same theme of the hidden yet pervasive growth of the kingdom of God ([ref:Luk 13:20-21|Luke 13:20-21]).
